The White-edged rockfish Sebastes taczanowskii is a viviparous scorpaenid inhabiting rocky reefs of the northwestern Pacific, where field surveys have documented a maximum recorded total length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters] among adults in the wild. This asymptotic size, derived from extensive sampling of mature individuals across the species range, places it among the smaller-bodied members of the subgenus Sebastodes. The fish is characterized by a moderately compressed body, spiny dorsal fin, and the mottled white-edged pigmentation that gives it its common name. Maturation in females occurs at a notably smaller size than the ultimate body length, with the first evidence of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis appearing at approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters] total length, a finding corroborated by histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected during the pre-spawning season. This size at puberty suggests that females invest approximately two years in somatic growth before diverting resources toward reproductive development, a pattern typical of slow-growing, long-lived rockfishes that face size-selective predation pressures as juveniles.

Neonatal body mass is remarkably low in this species, reflecting the highly altricial state of the larvae at parturition. Newborn individuals, following chorionase-mediated eclosion from the fertilized ovum within the maternal ovary, measure only 0.0003 grams [Wwb = 0.0003 grams] wet weight, a value that aligns closely with the birth masses reported for congeneric species such as Sebastes mentella, where egg diameter of approximately 0.833 millimeters drives comparably minute initial masses. This tiny alevin emerges from the follicle with a prominent yolk sac that sustains the endotrophic larva through the first several days of exogenous feeding, during which the mouth opens and first prey capture commences. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully mature, gravid females reaches up to 160 grams [Wwi = up to 160 grams], representing a five-order-of-magnitude increase from the birth mass. This dramatic ontogenetic trajectory underscores the species capacity for rapid mass accumulation during the juvenile phase before the energetic demands of reproduction and gonadal maturation begin to constrain further somatic growth.

Reproductive output in Sebastes taczanowskii has been quantified from captive broodstock maintained at a stable water temperature of 3.6 °C [T = 3.6 °C], conditions that approximate the thermal regime of their deep, subarctic habitat during the spawning season. Under these thermal conditions, females approaching the upper end of the adult size range—specifically those of approximately 48.3 centimeters total length—release an estimated 72,000 larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = an estimated 72,000 larvae per spawning event] annually, producing roughly one brood per year [F_R_i = roughly one brood per year]. This reproductive rate positions the White-edged rockfish as a moderately fecund iteroparous species, capable of generating substantial recruitment pulses despite extended inter-brood intervals. The relatively high fecundity per event likely represents an adaptation to compensate for elevated larval mortality in the planktonic phase, where ichthyoplankton face intense predation pressure and stochastic oceanographic conditions that can decimate cohort survival before the postflexion stage is reached.

Longevity records for this species, derived from otolith-based age validation studies of individuals captured in trawl surveys, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days] for populations inhabiting waters at 3.6 °C [T = 3.6 °C], the same thermal environment in which the reproductive observations were made. This translates to roughly eight years and underscores the life-history strategy of delayed maturation and slow growth typical of Sebastinae. The extended adult phase, during which females can contribute multiple annual broods, is critical for population persistence given the sporadic nature of successful larval recruitment in high-latitude shelf ecosystems. Comparative analyses reveal that S. taczanowskii achieves a slightly shorter lifespan than its deeper-dwelling congeners such as Sebastes alutus, which may exceed 20 years, but matches the longevity predicted by allometric scaling relationships for a species of its ultimate body length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a finding that reinforces links between maximum size and physiological aging rates in these rockfishes.

Habitat selection by juvenile S. taczanowskii following the pelagic-benthic transition involves a shift from the planktonic larval phase to structured benthic cover, where post-settlement individuals encounter a prey assemblage dominated by small crustaceans. The species thus progresses through a life cycle typical of demersal scorpaenids: an initial period of yolk dependency as a lecithotrophic prolarva, followed by the onset of exogenous feeding at the mouth-opening stage, a protracted phase of active growth in the pelagic ichthyoplankton community, and eventual settlement as a benthic juvenile. Field collections suggest that females become reproductively viable soon after reaching the 11-centimeter threshold (approximately 11 centimeters) [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters] for female puberty, after which they exhibit synchronous gonadal development each autumn. Ultimately, the combined evidence from body size distributions, reproductive output, and longevity records indicates that Sebastes taczanowskii follows a conservative, K-selected life-history strategy well suited to the cold, low-productivity waters of the northwestern Pacific continental shelf.
